event: VXE-820 (MOLSON) on 26 March 2026 did not have enough HLB charge to VTOL land at the HLZ because the fuel cell was not charging, so it was belly landed at the ELZ with minor composite damage.
component: SOFC cathode blower duct (HGS0794), fuel cell SN D4500799
failure_mode: Cathode blower duct came loose (adhesive failed), so the cathode fan could not cool the stack; the stack overheated, was damaged, ran at the voltage floor and minimum fuel and could not produce the power needed to charge the HLB.
contributing: duct retained only by adhesive with no mechanical retaining flange
low HLB state of charge at landing forced an ELZ glide landing

evidence.quote: Physical inspection of stack shows the cathode duct was not attached, explaining why even at maximum flow rates the cooling was ineffective
Cathode fan is unable to cool the stack
Lack of cooling damages stack, temperatures are not able to be maintained
Definite Stack Failure. The stack was not able to produce enough current, either from a short internally or a board issue that wasn’t allowing it to be asked to.
Redesigning HGS0794 (cathode blower duct) to have a redundant retaining flange to keep duct in place in the event of failure of adhesive.

team_root_cause: Cathode duct breaking creates conditions where the fan is unable to cool the stack causing failure.
attachments_read: 58508_CF-855-001 Return Material Authorization (RMA) Request Form - 820_930_929_fuel cell.pdf.md
reasoning: XCOMM log 129 shows the stack unable to produce current, running at the voltage floor and minimum fuel. The RCI presentation shows the stack never held 820C in warmup while cathode fan speed rose without effect, and physical inspection found the cathode duct detached. The corrective action (redesign of HGS0794 with a retaining flange because the adhesive can fail) confirms the duct retention as the starting point.
notes: Data confusion early on: the first AAR was the wrong flight, and Charles Sweet first reviewed XCL 121 to 128 before Cody Smisek pointed to XCOMM file 129. VXEP-1794 covers an earlier VXE-820 fuel cell charging complaint (23 March) closed as operating as designed. Intake PDF on RMA-970 and the RMA forms are blank or image only. A comment about closing via RMA-973 was retracted as meant for VXEP-1586.

event: VXE-828 (LRR, Block 35X) lost link after transition to fixed wing; the team put it down to RF interference on the Silvus frequency in use at the site.
failure_mode: Other emitters in the area on the same frequency stepped on the Silvus link, causing loss of link in fixed wing flight.
contributing: operators did not change frequency or run a spectrum scan on arrival at the mission site
supplied AAR data did not align with the reported flight

evidence.quote: The link loss on take was due to operators not changing freqs or conducting spectrum scan upon arriving to mission site.
had operators redo spectrum scan, operate in different frequencies
closing ticket due to provided Silvus troubleshooting. issue resolved
On hold for one week. The data doesn’t align to any of the flight data.

team_root_cause: Silvus was being stepped on due to freq in area

would_settle_it.what: Silvus link quality and noise floor around the transition to fixed wing, to confirm interference rather than a radio or antenna fault

would_settle_it.file: spectrum scan results from the site
would_settle_it.what: Whether other emitters occupied the original operating frequency

reasoning: The engineers state the link loss was caused by operators not changing frequency or running a spectrum scan at the site, and the issue cleared after a new spectrum scan and a change of frequency. No log analysis is shown and the supplied data did not match the flight, so the evidence reaches the radio link and RF environment but not a measured interference source.
notes: RMA-1067 describes a second, later event: VXE-828 lost link and GPS and crashed on 9 May 2026, with no data from the customer; the aircraft was replaced with V1059. That crash is not analyzed here. AAR zips are listed only. RMA PDFs are blank forms or image only scans.

event: LM UK (TIQUILA) reported arcing and damage on the AS150 power connector of VXE-672 and one other aircraft during connection; no flight event.
failure_mode: Arcing on mating that has damaged the contacts; suspected failed anti-spark resistor or a pin length tolerance that lets the main contact close before the resistor section.
contributing: known reliability history of these contacts (VXEP-553 systemic collector)

evidence.quote: We’ve had some reports of users experiencing connector arching.
Measure resistance of antispark resitor and dimensions vs drawing.
I think it should be replaced. Hard to measure or quantify risk to flight. These contacts have had reliability issues.

team_view_in_comments: this is likely caused by either a failure of the anti-spark resistor on the pin

would_settle_it.what: Photos of the damaged contacts, to see whether arc damage is on the anti-spark resistor pin or the main contact
Measure anti-spark resistor resistance and pin dimensions against the drawing

reasoning: The customer reports arcing and damage at the AS150 connector. The engineer offers two candidate mechanisms (failed anti-spark resistor, or tolerance letting the plus pin connect before the resistor section) but no measurement or teardown has been done. The evidence reaches the AS150 power contact but not which of the two mechanisms.
notes: Ticket covers two aircraft (VXE-672 and one not named). The only attachment (672 arching (2).docx) yielded no text. Which harness side (aircraft or battery) carries the damaged connector is not stated. VXEP-553 is an empty collector ticket.

event: VXE-620 (TIQUILA) after 2 h 10 min of flight transitioned to VTOL for recovery but the rear right lift motor never started, the aircraft spiraled down and was destroyed.
component: lift ESC or lift motor (rear right)
failure_mode: Motor did not start after transition with its command at maximum; no warning shown on the GCS; bench tests of the boom, ESCs, motors and center wing could not reproduce it and the ESC firmware read back identical to production.
contributing: no GCS warning or emergency indication of the failed motor
loss of one VTOL motor is not recoverable

evidence.quote: It is not spinning in the video and the commands for the RR are maxed out.
(4/23) Lawrence N: Connected CW to B30 IB, ran motor test for all 4 VTOL motors. All motors operated normally, performed wiggle test while operating which had no impact.
At the moment I don’t have any additional testing planned, and I was not able to recreate the failure.
But firmware corruption in the motor doesn't seem the cause.
HEAVY IMPACT AFTERVTOL, REAR RIGHT PROP FAILURE. AIRCRAFT DAMAGED BEYOND REPAIR

team_root_cause:
Unable to replicate so far. Firmware hangup seems like a more likely cause. Potentially due to corruption, but unable to determine. These are pretty rare, but have occurred before. 
B30 VTOL ESCs have had multiple failures. Tracking here https://jenaero.atlassian.net/browse/VXEP-628

would_settle_it.file: rear right lift ESC and motor
would_settle_it.what: Run the logged flight profile on the dyno with repeated cold starts after long cruise to catch an ESC processor hang
Boom, ESC enclosure and center wing test records and photos

reasoning: Logs and video show the rear right motor never spun up after transition while its command was maxed, which places the fault in the rear right motor or its ESC or their feed. Bench tests of the right boom, ESCs, motors and center wing wiring ran normally, and the ESC flash read back identical, so corruption looks unlikely. The team leans to an intermittent ESC firmware hang but could not reproduce it, so this stays narrowed.
notes: Root Cause field says unable to replicate and only suggests a firmware hang, so scored as no team answer. Customer documents call the aircraft battery configuration while the ticket says fuel cell. The two ESC flash dumps are avrdude logs and are identical except timing. DASOR PDF is photo captions only; intake PDF is image only.

event: VXE-658 (TIQUILA) on 30 March 2026 lost fuel cell power shortly after launch and returned on HLB power only.
component: fuel cell start sequence (initialized during cooldown), aircraft nose cone fan not enabled; FC SN D4500563
failure_mode: Fuel cell was initialized while still in cooldown (above 150C), faulted (critical fault 0x3c20), was restarted outside procedure, and in that state did not command the nose cone fan on; fuselage ambient rose above 85C and damaged the fuel cell electronics, cutting out the stack.
contributing: fuel cell and aircraft state logic did not enable the nose cone fan after the out of procedure restart (software gap, unresolved)

evidence.quote: The primary root cause of the failure is identified as an unconcluded cooldown cycle prior to initialization of the fuel cell.
Investigating the data shows that the vehicle’s nose cone fan was not initialized during the period of this flight.
In the beginning of XCL0042 we can see the stack state is still in cooldown, it looks like it was put into initialize before the stack was fully cooled down (CPU Time 515.549).
FanEn was set to 0 at startup of fuel cell in xcomm log 42 (dated 3/30/2026).
Seems we’ve got a software issue. I’d start chasing why did the fan enable set to off.

team_root_cause: The stack was still in cooldown when initialization was attempted, which caused a fault back into cooldown, then it was initialized a second time from cooldown and began normal operation except the nose cone fan never turned on causing damage to FC electronics.

would_settle_it.file: fuel cell and XCOMM state machine code
would_settle_it.what: Why the nose cone fan enable stays off when the stack is restarted from cooldown, to confirm whether software should have caught this

reasoning: XCOMM log 42 shows the stack moving directly from cooldown to initialize above 150C, a critical fault, then a second start, with FanEn at 0 for the flight. The investigation report links the missing nose cone fan to that out of procedure start and shows fuselage ambient above 85C damaging the fuel cell electronics. The start sequence is the trigger, but the software gap that let the fan stay off is not closed, so confidence is medium.
notes: Labels say Software and Cody Smisek pointed to a software state machine gap; the report puts it on operator procedure. Ticket resolution is Cannot Reproduce. Plot images are listed only.

event: VXE-622 (TIQUILA) avionics box could not connect to the GCS; on the ironbird the FWAP never came up, and swapping in a known good FWAP fixed it.
failure_mode: MPU-9250 initialization fails and the FWAP firmware loops retrying it, so the FWAP never reports and the GCS cannot connect; 5V to GND measured 320 ohms.
contributing: same failure found in VXE-655 (VXEP-1840), suggesting a lot or fleet issue
reflashing FWAP firmware did not help

evidence.quote: Swapped in AP SN:10877, confirmed issue resolved
Found that there is an issue with the MPU in both 622 and 655.
then goes into a while loop and continues to fail Init
Magfault alert comes in from XCOMM (signs of life)
Attempt to reflash FWAP to 6.5.0 v6.05s - same result “Failed to Connect”

team_view_in_comments: Evidence is consistent with MPU 9250 issue and needs to be replaced

would_settle_it.what: Shorting, FOD or corrosion under the shield, and CSAM for package delamination of the MPU-9250, to find why it failed

reasoning: On the ironbird the XCOMM was alive but the throughput page showed no FWAP data and reflashing the FWAP did not help. XCOMM logs show the MPU-9250 init failing in a loop, and swapping in a known good autopilot fixed the connection. That swap test plus the named log failure places the fault on the FWAP MPU-9250; why the part failed is still open.
notes: Both VXEP-1838 and VXEP-1840 carry the same Issue Status text including the same replacement AP SN 10877, apparently copied between tickets. The quote form attached to RMA-958 is filled in for A655 (RMA-960), an export or filing quirk. No Root Cause field.

event: VXE-648 (TIQUILA) could not connect normally; bench work found the XCOMM CAN transceiver damaged so VTOL AP data did not reach the XCOMM and AARs could not be downloaded.
failure_mode: CAN transceiver powered and receiving data but not outputting valid CAN frames to the rest of the aircraft.
contributing: cause of the transceiver damage not investigated; box not fully evaluated for other damage

evidence.quote: Appears that the CAN chip has been damaged somehow.
Although the CAN transceiver was correctly receiving power and data, it was not outputting appropriate CAN frames to the rest of the aircraft.
The MAX305 CAN transceiver was damaged.
The center wing was initially investigated. However, once the center wing successfully connected to a different avionics box, the investigation shifted to the avionics box and its internals.
After additional testing, connecting to the GCS does not seem to be the issue. It seems like there is an issue with CAN and downloading AARs

team_view_in_comments: Appears that the CAN chip has been damaged somehow.

would_settle_it.file: XCOMM board from VXE-648 avionics box
would_settle_it.what: Failure analysis of the CAN transceiver (overvoltage or ESD damage on the CAN lines) to find what damaged it

attachments_read: 64570_CF-820-014 RMA Quote Request Form A648 SPARE RMA 260407-2.docx.md
reasoning: The XCOMM VTOL page showed no VTOL AP data, and a bench CAN capture compared with a known good board showed the transceiver not sending proper frames. The center wing worked with another avionics box, isolating the fault to the avionics box, and the report names the XCOMM CAN transceiver. The part is identified, but what damaged it was never investigated.
notes: The report calls the part MAX305; that name is copied as written. FS2-4500 shows the box did connect to a GCS on the ironbird, with VTOL data coming from the ironbird, so "unable to connect" was really a CAN and AAR download problem. No Root Cause field; no formal investigation report beyond the slide deck.
